A student in Kathmandu asking an LLM to explain federalism, or a policymaker asking it to summarise arguments on land reform, is receiving an answer shaped by an invisible hand, one calibrated not in Kathmandu, Kavrepalanchok or Karnali, but somewhere between San Francisco and the aggregate preferences of anonymous human raters.

None of this makes artificial intelligence a threat to our opinions in itself. A well-written book, a persuasive newspaper column, even a charismatic teacher, can all shape a mind, and none of us calls for their banishment. The threat lies in the possibility that we stop noticing that these machines have a leaning. Human beings have always been the primary authors of their own convictions, sifting, doubting and occasionally reversing what they are told. That faculty does not become obsolete because a machine now answers faster and more fluently than any teacher or editor before it. It becomes more necessary than ever. The question, then, is not whether LLMs are setting up our political ideologies. It is whether we still remember how to ask them why.

articles.title: Nepal’s revived Industrial Security Force must ensure business protection
articles.summary:
The private sector has long served as the primary engine of the Nepali economy, generating approximately 86 percent of jobs and contributing roughly 81.55 percent to the national output. Yet, for decades, commercial enterprises have borne the brunt of broader political instability and social grievances, routinely finding themselves the first targets of arson, extortion and looting. Against this backdrop, the Government of Nepal’s recent decision to revive the Industrial Security Force (ISF) under the newly launched Private Investment Protection and Promotion Strategy is a welcome move.

Albeit late, the strategy represents the Balen Shah administration’s pragmatic shift towards acknowledging that capital accumulation cannot flourish if the physical security of enterprises is compromised. After recurring instances of civil unrest—most notably the Gen Z movement of September, which inflicted losses exceeding Rs84 billion to private businesses across the country, and the more recent arson of enterprises in Golbazar, Siraha, towards the end of July—the government seems to be attempting to rebuild the shattered confidence of the business community. This is also in line with PM Shah’s meeting with leaders of the business community on July 8.

The historical precedent of the ISF is deeply discouraging. The Armed Police Force personnel initially deployed under the ISF concept in 2012 were permanently redeployed to border regions during the Covid-19 pandemic and never returned to their industrial posts. This security vacuum, even after the pandemic ended, left major industrial corridors completely vulnerable, inducing a climate of persistent risk that stagnated private investment growth at a dismal 0.2 percent in the last fiscal year.

While declaring industrial zones as ‘peace zones’ and establishing rapid-response teams are commendable policy steps, such strategic formulation alone will not assuage the deep-seated investor scepticism. Timely amendments to laws such as the Industrial Enterprises Act, the Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act, and the Special Economic Zone Act also help the cause by demonstrating commendable legislative intent. However, the introduction of security strategies remains mere symbolism until the government demonstrates a resolute zero-tolerance stance against offenders through actual prosecution and punishment. The Shah administration’s ambitious economic targets—expanding the national economy to nearly $100 billion, raising per capita income to $3,000, and maintaining an average annual growth rate of 7 percent—will remain entirely unachievable if the state fails to guarantee basic property rights and physical safety.

To convert the strategic initiative of ISF into a tangible economic catalyst, the Shah government must focus on decisive, multi-layered execution. First, the deployment of the revived security force must be institutionalised through dedicated, permanent units, ensuring that personnel are never again diverted to auxiliary state duties during crises. Second, the state must establish a clear legal precedent of accountability. Legal proceedings against individuals involved in commercial vandalism must be swift, resolute and transparent, ending the decades-long culture of impunity that has surrounded targeted attacks on private enterprises.

Furthermore, the government should swiftly operationalise the proposed joint coordination and facilitation committee comprising state officials and private-sector representatives. It is incumbent that this framework empowers business leaders to directly highlight emerging security vulnerabilities before localised protests escalate into destructive violence. Combining these security measures with proactive administrative relief—such as streamlining relocation permits through Initial Environmental Examinations for damaged businesses and granting targeted tax, fee, or penalty waivers for struggling firms—will provide immediate support to the commercial landscape. Ultimately, policy declarations must translate into tangible protection on the ground. Only by guaranteeing a safe, predictable and resilient operational environment can Nepal inspire domestic enterprise, attract foreign direct investment, and place its national economy on a sustainable trajectory toward long-term prosperity.

articles.title: Building a tax system for trust, investment and prosperity
articles.summary:
The 2026-27 fiscal budget deserves appreciation for one important reason. Amid competing fiscal pressures and slowing economic activity, it has committed to launching a second generation of tax reforms. The timing could not be more appropriate. Nepal’s tax system has reached a stage where incremental changes are no longer sufficient. What is now required is a comprehensive reform agenda that restores public trust, promotes investment, broadens the tax base, and prepares the country for a rapidly changing economy.

But despite all the promise and hype around tax reforms with the change in government, there are signals of policy flip-flops, unpredictability, loss of trust, and even backsliding of earlier reforms. This is especially true with the probability of introducing multiple Value Added Tax (VAT) rates (for example, a different rate of 5 percent on electricity) and losing the fairness and equity—both horizontal and vertical—elements in the new tax tariffs or administrative measures. Moreover, the government has introduced several new tax concessions and exemptions (as summarised in sections 68 and 73 of the Budget Speech 2083–84) despite the promise of comprehensive application of the tax regime to broaden the tax base.

Nepal is not starting from scratch. The country has already witnessed the first generation of tax reforms in the 1990s. The reforms introduced in that period had three landmark departures from the earlier tax regime. First, self-assessment in income taxation shifted the relationship between taxpayers and the tax administration from official determination to voluntary compliance. Second, the introduction of a single-rate VAT, an input tax credit mechanism, and a built-in self-policing system created one of the most efficient indirect tax structures. Third, self-declaration in customs and excise moved tax administration away from excessive official discretion towards greater trust in taxpayers.

These reforms were guided by a simple philosophy: lower tax rates, a broader tax base, and greater tax equity. Moderate, universally applied tax rates were expected to encourage compliance, reduce tax evasion, and generate higher revenues without discouraging investment and economic growth. For many years, this framework served Nepal well.

The challenge today is not that the original reforms were flawed, but that their underlying principles have gradually been diluted. Over the years, substantive tax laws have increasingly been amended through annual finance acts. Frequent policy changes have depleted trust in the tax system by introducing uncertainty and unpredictability, and have made long-term business and investment decisions difficult. Equally concerning has been the proliferation of tax exemptions and concessions. Every exemption narrows the tax base, creates opportunities for leakage, and often rewards influence rather than genuine economic merit.

At the same time, tax procedures have failed to modernise to meet the needs of a digital economy. Compliance remains costly and cumbersome. Excessive paperwork, multiple reporting requirements, and outdated administrative practices increase the cost of doing business. These weaknesses have adversely affected investment, productivity, growth and employment.

Tax Reform 2.0 must, therefore, begin by restoring trust. No tax system can function efficiently unless taxpayers have confidence that tax laws are predictable, fairly administered and consistently applied. Predictability, policy stability, impartial administration and transparency should become the cornerstones of Nepal’s tax system.

Tax administration itself requires fundamental modernisation. Paperless and contactless procedures should become the norm. Full self-assessment, supported by risk-based audits and digital verification, can significantly reduce compliance costs while improving administrative efficiency. Honest taxpayers should find compliance easier, while deliberate non-compliance should become increasingly difficult through intelligent data analysis rather than excessive physical enforcement.

A comprehensive review of tax exemptions is equally essential. Most concessions should either be eliminated or subjected to transparent public disclosure through annual tax expenditure statements. Tax equity must guide reform once again. Horizontal equity requires taxpayers with similar economic capacity to bear similar tax burdens. Vertical equity demands protection of lower-income households from excessive tax incidence. Where environmental taxes such as carbon taxes are introduced, targeted budgetary compensation should protect poorer households from their regressive effects.

Digital economic activities should be brought under a tax framework by subjecting such transactions to both direct and indirect taxes based upon emerging international practices. Likewise, informal businesses should gradually be integrated into the formal tax system initially at low tax rates and with simplified procedures to formalise the economy and expand the tax base.

Technology should become the backbone of modern tax administration. Integrated databases capable of communicating with banking systems, business registries and other government databases can verify transactions intelligently while reducing unnecessary compliance costs. Artificial intelligence and advanced analytics can improve audit selection, detect fraud and strengthen revenue administration. Such modernisation requires sustained investment in reliable hardware, secure software and skilled human resources.

Tax reform must also reflect Nepal’s federal governance structure. Tax procedures should be harmonised across federal, provincial and local governments to provide an integrated nationwide tax framework to the taxpayers. Double taxation of the same transaction should be eliminated while ensuring fair revenue sharing among all three levels of government. The indirect tax structure also deserves careful review. Preserving a single VAT rate maintains simplicity and minimises disputes, while a modest reduction in the rate, combined with a broader tax base and improved compliance, could stimulate economic activity without compromising revenue.

Revenue reform should extend beyond taxation alone. Better management of non-tax revenues—including market-based pricing of natural resources, fair returns from public assets, improved utilisation of public infrastructure, and modern cash management through short-term treasury instruments—can significantly strengthen public finances.

Ultimately, tax reform is about rebuilding the social contract between the state and its citizens. People are more willing to pay taxes when they see that public resources are managed efficiently, transparently and for the common good.

A second generation of tax reform will undoubtedly demand strong commitment at both the political and organisational levels. There are no gains without pains. Every meaningful reform temporarily disrupts established interests as it realigns resources, priorities and economic and social structures. It therefore requires careful management of the political economy of reform and sustained leadership to overcome inevitable resistance.

Yet, the long-term rewards far outweigh the short-term costs. A good tax system is not one that simply collects more revenue; it is one that releases the productive resources of businesses for greater investment, innovation and employment while ensuring fairness for all. In an ideal economy, investment decisions should be driven by the economic merits of the investment itself—not by tax distortions or preferential treatments. That should be the true objective of Tax Reform 2.0.

articles.title: How US military funding propelled China’s robot dogs
articles.summary:
China’s Unitree Robotics – among the world’s biggest producers of humanoid and quadruped robots – based designs for its most successful robot dogs on innovations funded by the US military, according to a former US defence technology official and three top researchers involved in the project.

Unitree’s $1,600 Go2 model, launched in 2023, helped the company rapidly dominate the global quadruped robot market — its Shanghai IPO has drawn frenzied demand. Another Unitree robot has been shown on Chinese state television armed and accompanying People’s Liberation Army (PLA) troops on an exercise.

These robots draw on breakthroughs in quadruped movement financed by the US DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory (ARL) and other military programs, the researchers and the former official told Reuters.

The Army-funded project turned into, “basically, the first Unitree robot that had any kind of scale,” said Gavin Kenneally, a former University of Pennsylvania researcher involved in the program.

Ben Katz, who worked at Massachusetts Institute of ‌Technology’s Biomimetic Robotics Lab, among a consortium of universities financed by the military programs, said the dimensions of Unitree’s popular Go series were “to the millimetre” almost identical to a groundbreaking robot he helped develop called Mini Cheetah.

Reuters is the first media outlet to detail connections between Unitree designs and the Army program.

The episode underscores broader problems with the United States’ ability to compete with China’s state-directed manufacturing sector in high-tech strategic industries, including those critical to national security. Backed by subsidies, clusters of component factories, and a tolerance for heavy losses, Chinese companies have seized market share across industries such as solar panels, drones, EVs and quantum communications, many of which were first developed in the US with government or military backing.

Kenneally commercialised the US breakthroughs through his company Ghost Robotics, which supplies US special forces with advanced, ruggedised robots. But compared to Unitree, its production is small, and costly.

In June, the Pentagon added Unitree to a list of Chinese military companies, calling it a “contributor to the Chinese defence industrial base.” That designation falls short of a sanction but limits the US military’s future use of Unitree’s technology. Unitree has said its robots are for civilian use.

Unitree, China’s State Council and China’s defence ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

Unitree did nothing underhanded in using the US Army research. The program’s findings were published openly to stimulate progress in the field, a common practice.

ARL spokesperson Amanda Ligon said the research “strengthened the broader US robotics ecosystem” and informed subsequent work across government and the private sector.

ARL referred questions about Unitree’s commercialisation of the technology to the Pentagon, which declined to comment.

US companies vs. China industrial policy

Unitree sold more ⁠than 5,500 humanoids and 18,000 quadrupeds last year, company filings show, and it’s now valued at about $9 billion ahead of its stock market debut on Wednesday.

By contrast, no US company has mass-produced such robots, including Elon Musk’s Tesla, which has displayed prototypes of its Optimus humanoid for years. On a January earnings call, Musk called China “incredibly good” at scaling production.

Boston Dynamics, the US company whose 2019 canine, Spot, used different technology, recently argued in a Congressional hearing that China’s low pricing would drive US firms out of the market.

None of the US robotics researchers who spoke with Reuters advocated for keeping such government-financed research secret. Instead, they said, US policymakers should focus on enabling companies to quickly commercialise such advances to compete with China.

ARL also said publication was important to scientific and technological advancement.

The US excels in innovation and software development but needs to ensure the capital, industrial base, highly skilled workforce and parts supply chains to scale up breakthroughs, said Vijay Kumar, dean at Penn Engineering.

For now, US authorities often protect companies with trade restrictions on innovative Chinese products. In July, the Federal Communications Commission banned imports of future models of foreign-made humanoid and quadruped robots, including those from Unitree. China has threatened to retaliate to the FCC ban.

China’s Washington embassy said in a statement its companies are making new technologies affordable and accessible internationally. It accused the US of abusing administrative power, and of “market distortion and unilateral bullying.”

Most of the experts who spoke to Reuters supported the US ban but said the policy is not enough to build an industry to catch up with China.

“This isn’t just a competition between US and Chinese robotics companies,” said Kenneally, the Ghost Robotics founder. “It’s between private US companies and China’s coordinated national strategy.”

In 2015, Chinese President Xi Jinping set out a 10-year plan to lead industries including green energy, electric vehicles and robotics. Since then, China has channelled capital into risky bets on low-margin 21st-century advanced manufacturing.

Chinese robot manufacturers’ rapid reverse-engineering of products draws on the country’s dominance in refining critical minerals needed for magnets in robotics applications and the density of suppliers of motors, gears, ‘muscles’ known as actuators, and other components clustered near Unitree’s base in Hangzhou.

Reyk Knuhtsen, a robotics analyst at SemiAnalysis, called the United States’ failure to commercialise domestic research a “dropped ball,” citing US venture capital’s preference for high-return software startups. It would take more than trade barriers on China to boost robotics manufacturing, he said.

“This is a very big hill for the US to climb,” he said.

The White House did not respond to requests for comment about US industrial policy. An FCC spokesperson said the commission was protecting Americans from foreign threats and preparing the country “to deliver on President ‌Trump’s vision to lead ⁠the world on the next generation of technologies.”

Jaret Riddick, who as a former Army Research Laboratory director oversaw the Army-funded robotics project, said it did kick-start the US quadruped industry. But in the end, without support for large-scale production, Unitree in China “just kind of consumed that space.”

Teaching robot dogs new tricks

The Army funded the Robotics Collaborative Technology Alliance (RCTA) between 2010 and 2020.

The RCTA gathered government, academic and industry researchers from UPenn, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Boston Dynamics, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, and other research institutions. The alliance’s top commercial partner was General Dynamics Land Systems, the Michigan-based defense manufacturer that makes Abrams M1 tanks.

In 2016, UPenn researchers, including Kenneally, eliminated heavy central gearboxes and placed motors in robots’ legs, enhancing the ability to sense and respond to terrain. UPenn’s progress built on the MIT lab’s work funded by the Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA).

In 2019, the MIT lab presented the Mini Cheetah, building on UPenn features with increased strength – and the ability to do backflips.

Months earlier, Katz published his MIT master's thesis, detailing Mini Cheetah’s actuators. Within six months, he found Chinese companies manufacturing actuator copies “you could buy on AliExpress,” he said, referring to the Chinese online retail giant.

Unitree had been founded three years before by Wang Xingxing, then 26 years old. In his 2016 master’s thesis from Shanghai University, which Reuters reviewed online, Wang cited the work done at MIT, including on earlier iterations of the Cheetah, and set out principles consistent with those ⁠developed at the US lab. He acknowledged the lab’s “pioneering” contributions.

In his thesis, Wang explored design tweaks to speed up development, saying his findings could have future “defence, security, family and education” applications. He referenced Kenneally’s ARL-funded UPenn paper.

On its website, Unitree says the company “independently developed the motors, reducers, controllers, and even some sensors of the quadruped robot.”

Katz told Reuters he decided against taking his actuators into production, thinking there would be no market. He said China’s ability to move fast had broad benefits: Robotics “has advanced a lot because of the availability of actuators.”

Joao Ramos, who did research at the same time as Katz at the MIT lab, said Unitree copied the Mini Cheetah shape, structure and design. But he credited the company with doing “proper engineering” to perfect a mass-produced robot.

“The actual practical implementation, bringing it to real life, that’s all on them,” Ramos said.

Gun-toting robot dogs

Walking robots aren’t yet widely deployed on battlefields, but the United States and Chinese militaries have both explored the prospect. ⁠In October, another Chinese company’s “Robot Wolf” quadrupeds featured in Chinese media coverage of the PLA conducting mock beach landings,

Unitree has said in public statements that its products are intended for civilian use. In 2022, the company signed an open letter along with US companies pledging not to weaponise robots, citing risks of harm and serious ethical issues.

But Chinese state television has featured Unitree’s Go2 model robots alongside Chinese troops and a modified version of the firm’s B1 series robot firing a mounted assault rifle.

In September 2023, the US Army secured a federal waiver from laws requiring government agencies to prioritise American-made products, in order to purchase two Unitree Go2s, according to procurement records that described the devices as crucial tools in the absence of sufficient commercial quantities of US-produced alternatives “of a satisfactory quality.” Reuters could not establish whether the purchases went ahead.

Later that month, US Marines conducted an exercise attaching a rocket launcher to a Go1 ⁠to enable remote firing.

Kenneally’s Ghost Robotics has shipped about 1,000 of its Vision 60 robots, mostly to military and government customers for surveillance and search applications in harsh environments. The company’s first customer was Navy Special Warfare Command, which oversees Navy SEAL teams.

Some components for the Vision 60s, which sell for upwards of $165,000, are built in China, though the company has sought to move its supply chain. By comparison, Unitree lists its B series robot for below $100,000 in the US

Ghost Robotics shifted its motor supply from China to South Korea two years ago, though it still finds it difficult to eliminate Chinese magnets and some metal components, Kenneally said.

The only way to escape China’s chokehold on the robotics supply chain, he said, is to secure supplies from other countries that have the manufacturing capacity that the United States lacks. In 2024, South Korea’s LIG Defence & Aerospace acquired a 60% stake in Ghost Robotics for $240 million. The company is exploring production in Taiwan, Kenneally said.

“We need to work closely with our allies,” he said. “There’s absolutely no path forward without them.”

articles.title: Movie review: In ‘Chiso Maanchhe’, a journey with a corpse becomes a meditation on grief and human connection
articles.summary:
There are not many Nepali filmmakers willing to trust their audience to understand their film without announcing its intentions through dialogues. Dipendra K Khanal, however, seems to have given us a space to sit with his images, silences and ambiguities to make sense of ‘Chiso Maanchhe’ on our own.

Released in the theatres in 2022 and on YouTube in 2025, the film begins with a rolling wheel as the radio announces the number of deaths in Nepal during the coronavirus pandemic. Ashok (played by Arpan Thapa) has a mask hanging under his chin and a sanitiser on the edge of his truck’s window.

Ashok, a driver, is hired to take a corpse from Kathmandu to Bajura in his truck. This is a corpse that has freshly arrived from Qatar, one of the major destinations for Nepali migrant workers. Accompanying Ashok are a grieving father, Sher Bahadur (Deshbhakta Khanal), and a widowed wife (Swastima Khadka). The wheels roll and the journey begins.

As they travel from Kathmandu to Bajura, they encounter the broader terror of the widespread virus with the roads engulfed by corpses, migrants, police, and youth patrols. Some go along with them and others obstruct their passage.

With them moving, stopping, negotiating, rebelling and starting again, the story becomes an emblem of the precariousness of life. Along with this, the characters, initially entirely as strangers, begin to understand each other’s worlds, and more importantly, their own.

Khanal, also the director of ‘Aama’, ‘Pashupati Prasad’, ‘Ke Ghar Ke Dera’, is best known for depicting social issues and everyday struggles in his films and he continues doing so in ‘Chiso Maanchhe’. The film shows a broader picture of a frozen, individualistic and isolated society.

In a scene, Khadka’s character is found frolicking in the woods, as though she stumbled upon an oasis. Her father-in-law calls her out, quickly and furiously, and says, “If this was the old days, you would’ve had to become a sati.” The sati is a historical custom where a widow self-immolates on her deceased husband’s funeral pyre.

“If not physically, I have been made a sati in heart,” she says.

It is a line the film never explains, and doesn't need to, because by then, Khanal has already taught us to read what isn't said. Non-verbal cues in the film stand monumental for its provocative ways to communicate its themes and the characters’ emotions.

The truck carrying the corpse of Damber Bahadur, who died of “heart failure” in Qatar, has a quote painted on its back in red. “Life goes on with happiness and laughter. If we work hard, we can find gold in our own country.”

The irony is stark and unmistakable.

Further, these non-verbal cues particularly elaborate the dynamics between Ashok, the driver, and the daughter-in-law.

Whether it’s buying her a bag of titaura to satisfy her cravings or extinguishing his cigarette when she looks uncomfortable, these small, wordless gestures create a sense of intimacy throughout their journey.

With this screenwriting, as commendable as to earn him the ‘Best Writer Award’ for the film, Khanal, however, fails to depict the nuances of his female character. He neither gives a promising background to the daughter-in-law nor a name.

Khadka’s character attempts to run away before retrieving her husband’s dead body. Later, she is found staring at a poster that showed the winner of ‘Nepal Idol’, a singing reality show. We understand consequently that her dream was to become a singer, and that the marriage had not given her enough reasons to grieve her dead husband.

She is given a dream. And a somewhat rebellious nature to chase it. But not enough to earn her a platform of her own.

However, Khadka’s body language, dialect, eye contacts, and even the way she blinks are carefully curated habits to build her character which results in a memorable depiction despite being written unidimensionally.

Ashok, on the other hand, gets to reminisce about his dead wife and six-month-old child whom he left behind with his sister. We understand his financial struggles after he receives a call from his bank warning about the confiscation of his vehicle.

Ashok’s cognitive understanding of self and emotional intelligence add depth to his character.

Costumes of the three lead characters, which are the same throughout the film along with their make-up, also amplify the realism of the film, fitting perfectly into the travel-cinema narrative.

Khanal knew his ways to create a connection between the audience and the screen. With minimal dialogues, the audience, from early on, can get the idea of having to pay close attention to the cinematography, colours, props, and every edge of a frame.

One that stands out the most is the red light inside the truck juxtaposed by the darkness of the outside. Ambience as such gives the film a sense of depth under the warmth, or the discomfort of red.

However, at times, it is almost difficult to put into words the intent of the director. One is compelled to replay some scenes over and over again, simply to understand its underlying motive.

There’s a scene, for instance, where a line of people wearing masks and carrying their belongings walk in a corner of a moving frame. But it is not clear what Khanal is trying to imply with it. After all, why were the people there? Why in a single line? Why were they carrying their belongings and where were they going? Questions like these remain unanswered.

This ambiguity further enters the moral terrain inhabited by the film’s characters. Scenes of dispute and altercation also follow the journey. Yet, every character is given their own motivation and moral ground, resisting the easy division between right and wrong.

Therefore, the film pivots toward a moral question. And Sher Bahadur seems to be the most affected by it. His character, initially a grieving father and a culturally restrictive father-in-law, slowly melts into a man capable of introspection.

‘Chiso Maanchhe’ may seem like it has a slow pace. And it certainly does. But rather than a drawback, it is the film’s conscious choice to demand patience from its viewers.

In the end, the film leaves a corpse, an unrequited love, and a society in transition. It asks us to sit in the cold with its characters. Perhaps the coldness is not only theirs.

articles.title: How Dijup Tuladhar uses AI as part of his everyday toolkit
articles.summary:
Working in US healthcare means I frequently encounter terminology and systems that are unfamiliar in the Nepali context. Previously, understanding a new healthcare concept could require hours or days. Now, I can use AI to break down unfamiliar concepts.

I still verify important information through reliable sources. But AI has shortened the distance.

Building Chordpedia

I founded Chordpedia in 2015 after struggling to find chords for Nepali songs online. The biggest challenge was always execution. AI has changed that equation.

With AI-assisted coding and tools such as ChatGPT, I can move from an idea to a prototype or working feature much faster.

Design and prototyping

Tools such as Figma Make, Lovable and Stitch have changed how I move from an idea to something tangible.

Previously, there was a long process between having an idea and being able to interact with a prototype. Now, I can describe a problem, explore different approaches, generate a prototype, interact with it, identify problems and make changes almost immediately.

However, AI has made the process of designing faster yet hasn't necessarily made deciding what to design easier.

User research and feedback

I use AI to process large amounts of user feedback and identify patterns. It can group similar responses, summarise what users are saying and help him look at competitors from different perspectives.

I look at AI as an assistant. AI can help identify patterns and ask questions, but it cannot always understand the context behind a decision—including users, business priorities, organisational culture and technical limitations.

Everyday life

AI is not limited to my professional life. I also use it for travel planning, learning, comparing options and solving technical problems.

One of my favourite things to do is to use AI to challenge my own thinking.

Instead of asking AI to agree with an idea, I ask it to explain why the idea might be wrong, what I could be missing and what an opposing perspective might look like.

articles.title: Nepal, India to discuss cross-border security concerns tomorrow
articles.summary:
Senior home ministry officials from Nepal and India will meet in Dehradun, India, on Thursday and Friday for talks on border management and a range of bilateral security concerns, amid heightened attention to security along the two countries’ open and porous border.

The 14th meeting of the India-Nepal Joint Working Group on Border Management comes in the wake of recent unrest and communal violence in Nepal’s Tarai-Madhesh region, which shares a long border with India.

Although Nepal’s security agencies have found no credible evidence of direct or indirect links between the unrest and individuals or groups operating from India, border security and other cross-border concerns are expected to feature prominently in the talks, a senior home ministry official told the Post.

“The discussions are expected to cover issues such as religious fundamentalism, the activities of third-country nationals who could potentially be involved in instigating unrest, and monitoring their movements,” said the official.

Anand Kafle, joint secretary at the home ministry who oversees the Security and Coordination Division, will lead the Nepali delegation at the two-day annual meeting.

The ministry officials say the agenda includes cross-border criminal activities, the entry and movement of third-country nationals, smuggling, drug trafficking from India into Nepal and illegal trade in arms and ammunition.

Circulation of counterfeit currency, information sharing between the security agencies of Nepal and India, border regulations, removal of encroachments in no-man’s land, and unauthorised trade are the other agenda.

Also on the agenda are Indian assistance to Nepali security agencies, information sharing, capacity building of Nepal’s security institutions, and Nepal’s request for India to recognise its national identity card as a valid travel document.

The two sides will also review decisions taken by lower-level security mechanisms involving chief district officers on the Nepali side and district magistrates on the Indian side, as well as the Armed Police Force and India’s Sashastra Seema Bal.

“Since 2010, we have discussed religious fundamentalism, the role of third-country nationals in instigating unrest, illegal border crossings and information sharing on related matters in every meeting. We expect similar discussions this time too,” the ministry official said.

“But we are not in a position to provide any concrete evidence to the Indian side that any group or individual was involved in instigating the unrest in the Tarai-Madhesh.”

Within Nepal’s security apparatus, however, there is some apprehension that certain individuals and groups operating in India and other third countries could have strong religious or other links that may have contributed to the recent unrest.

Issues concerning radical and religious fundamentalism, the activities of third-country nationals across the border and tightening border security have routinely featured in security meetings between the two countries, ranging from the home secretary level to meetings between chief district officers and district magistrates.

Nepal and India also have a permanent local-level mechanism, the Border District Coordination Committee (BDCC), to address security issues in border districts.

“In every security-related meeting, officials from both sides discuss the risks posed by third-country nationals, religious fundamentalism and radical elements, but we have hardly been able to do anything about them,” a former Nepal Police official said.

Some of the issues on the agenda are permanent, officials said. The meeting will also review progress made since the 13th meeting, held in Pokhara last year.

Since the Boundary Working Group and the Survey Officials Committee began meeting regularly, the mandate and work of these two boundary-related mechanisms have also occasionally featured in discussions.

In earlier meetings, officials discussed the repair and maintenance of border pillars, particularly in the absence of regular meetings of the two boundary-related mechanisms.

This time, too, officials are expected to discuss trans-border criminal activities; strengthening border infrastructure, particularly integrated check posts, roads and railway networks; empowerment and capacity building of various security-related institutions; and ways to strengthen cooperation in disaster risk reduction and management.

articles.title: UML dissidents embrace the ‘awara’ label, launch ‘Awara Campaign’
articles.summary:
An unusual tea-drinking campaign is brewing inside the CPN-UML after Chairman KP Sharma Oli used the words ‘awara’ and ‘uranthheula’ for party leaders and activists calling for changes in policy and leadership. Both of these are derogatory Nepali words—awara, derived from the Persian language, translates roughly to ‘aimless drifter; while uranthheula means immature or frivolous.

On Tuesday afternoon, several senior UML leaders were laughing over tea at the party’s Chyasal canteen in Lalitpur. The ordinary act of ordering tea had become politically charged after Oli said that some people sitting in the party office canteen and discussing his removal were awara and uranthheula.

Oli’s remarks have angered leaders seeking an overhaul in party leadership, prompting the UML Intellectual Council’s ‘Revival Campaign’ to launch a satirical ‘Awara Campaign’.

The campaign mirrors India’s ‘cockroach movement,’ where activists turned an insult from the Chief Justice into a political campaign. But unlike the Indian movement, which escalated into nationwide protests, the Nepali campaign focuses on internal party reform.

“Let all the awaras across the country come together and go to the party office in Chyasal to drink tea,” the Awara Campaign says. Gajendra Thapaliya, who heads the council, said the initiative was organised by leaders and activists supporting party restructuring. “We have launched the Awara Campaign across the country for party restructuring,” he announced.

The organisers have prepared a graphic, inviting supporters to Chyasal for tea, turning Oli’s insult into a political slogan. This is not the first time UML activists have responded to criticism through humour and satire. Before the Gen Z movement, when UML leaders and cadres were labelled ‘jhole’, they launched a campaign declaring, “I am a UML jhole.”

The latest episode is part of a growing dispute over whether the UML needs changes in policy and leadership following its poor performance in the March 5 election.

Several senior leaders—including vice-chairs Bishnu Paudel, Gokarna Bista, Prithvi Subba Gurung and Raghuji Pant, general secretary Shankar Pokharel and deputy general secretary Yogesh Bhattarai—have been discussing organisational reform, according to party insiders.

The debate has sharpened after a task force led by vice-chair Ram Bahadur Thapa reviewed the election defeat and proposed changes to the party’s policies and leadership. Pokharel, who served as the task force’s secretary, prepared the report, which was submitted to Oli. Leaders involved in the process say it has not been acted upon and the task force has not met since.

Pokharel has gone further, calling for a special general convention to amend the party statute and then restructure the leadership. He has argued that the UML must examine why voters from grassroots social and economic groups have moved away from the party and why young people have fewer opportunities inside its organisation.

“The classes and communities in the grassroots moved away from the communist party when it was in government,” Pokharel wrote on Facebook. “Why did this happen, and why did the enthusiasm among leaders and cadres for social change weaken?”

Pokharel added a serious review of these questions was essential for the revival of the communist movement.

His position has put him at greater distance from Oli, despite having been one of the chairman’s closest political allies.

Oli has publicly rejected the demand for restructuring. Speaking in his home district Jhapa on Sunday, he said the party did not need restructuring but revival.

“Restructuring means making the policy, destination, struggle and programme new,” Oli said. “This is not the time for restructuring; it is the time for revival.”

Oli made his ‘awara’ remarks at an event in Ilam the same day. “Some awaras sit in the party office canteen and talk about removing the party chairman. Is that a joke?” he said. “Some people are walking around collecting signatures to remove the chairman. There is no substance behind this.”

The remarks have not gone down well with some UML leaders. Central committee member Anand Prasad Pokharel described the language as unfortunate. “The suggestion for policy and leadership restructuring came from the task force and is now being raised by cadres at the grassroots,” he said. “The remarks seem to have been made as if the restructuring demand were directed personally against him.”

Khimlal Bhattarai, another central committee member, said such language would make the dispute harder to resolve. “Such words do not solve the problem,” he said. “They make it more complicated.”

articles.title: Flu and fever spread in Jajarkot camps sheltering Saturday’s landslide survivors
articles.summary:
Dozens of landslide survivors in Jajarkot have fallen ill with flu and fever, officials say, as 691 people displaced by Saturday’s landslides were forced to take shelter at temporary camps in Bheri Municipality’s wards 2 and 3.

Doctors from the Provincial Hospital Surkhet reached the camps and treated 90 people on Monday.

“Ensuring safe drinking water has become a big challenge in the camps,” said Nisha Thapa, a public health inspector serving in the municipality. “Rainwater has contaminated almost all drinking water sources.”

At least four people died and half a dozen others were injured in the landslides that devastated entire villages in the municipality’s wards 1, 2, 3, and 4 on Saturday evening.

Elderly people, small children, pregnant women, and new mothers living in the camps are among those particularly vulnerable to water-borne and vector-borne diseases, Thapa said.

“The risk of illness spreading is high in the camps,” she said. Health workers serving in the municipality have set up a health desk at the encampment. “But that alone won’t be sufficient to address all the emerging problems.”

Municipal officials say the authorities are still unable to bury the cattle and other animals that perished in the landslides and warned of a heightened risk of a disease outbreak.

“The risk of disease spreading due to rotting carcasses has increased,” said Yagya Nath Gautam, chief of the disaster section of the municipality. Nepal Police, Armed Police Force and Nepali Army personnel have started burying the dead animals, he said.

Local authorities have set up a few makeshift toilets near the encampment but they are not sufficient for hundreds of the displaced. As a result many have been defecating in the open.

Open defecation risks further contaminating the water sources, officials said.

Experts also warn that the risk of vector-borne diseases, including malaria, dengue, kala-azar and scrub typhus, has increased.

“A major outbreak has not occurred yet, and we can handle the situation until next week,” Gautam said. “But after then, we would need support from the provincial and federal government.”

The disaster has displaced people from over 450 households who are taking refuge in temporary shelters or relatives’ houses.

Municipal officials say entire villages, devastated first by an earthquake some three years ago, and now by the landslide, need to be relocated to safer places.

At least 157 people died, hundreds were injured, and thousands were displaced by a magnitude 6.4 earthquake that hit Jajarkot and West Rukum in November 2023.

Preventing possible outbreaks of communicable diseases—water-borne and vector-borne—is the main challenge for now in areas affected by the landslides, said Dr Amrit Pokhrel, chief of the Emergency and Outbreak Management Section at the Epidemiology and Disease Control Division.

“We have been taking real-time updates on the developing situation,” Pokhrel said.

Jajarkot is among Nepal’s least developed districts. The district’s Human Development Index is below the national average. With poor nutrition, social, and educational standards in the district, experts warn of a high risk of major disease outbreaks soon.

Dr Baburam Marasini, a public health expert, said federal government agencies must act immediately, as local and provincial governments do not have the capacity to respond to a major disaster.

Jajarkot has a history of dealing with major communicable diseases. The district witnessed a cholera outbreak in 2009 that left several people dead and hundreds infected. A swine flu outbreak in 2015 similarly saw several dead and hundreds infected.

Experts have asked authorities to ensure hygienic food and safe drinking water for the displaced. They have also warned against relying on cheap junk foods like noodles and biscuits in the aftermath of disasters.

There are pregnant women, new mothers, small children and elderly people in the displaced camps, Marasini said, adding authorities should take prompt action. “Otherwise, those left behind by landslides will die from water-borne diseases,” he said.

articles.title: Gundruk turns into a business lifeline for women in Hetauda
articles.summary:
For generations, women in Ghale Gaun, a settlement in Hetauda-12, made gundruk as a way to preserve mustard greens for the winter. The greens were wilted, fermented in earthen pots and sun-dried before being stored for months.

The fermented greens were a staple in rural Nepali kitchens, but rarely seen as a source of income. That is changing.

Gundruk has gradually become the signature product of Ghale Gaun, giving the area a new identity as ‘Gundruk village’. Women who once spent most of their time on unpaid household and farm work now run a growing enterprise that covers everything from cultivating mustard greens to fermentation, packaging and marketing.

The transformation began three years ago when women, most of them from the Gurung and Tamang communities, organised themselves through the Kanchanjunga Agriculture Cooperative Micro-Entrepreneur Industry. They began cultivating mustard greens collectively for commercial gundruk production.

Their product later received organic certification from the government’s Department of Food Technology and Quality Control, helping boost consumer confidence and demand.

The increase in sales has been rapid. The cooperative sold 500 kilogrammes of gundruk in its first year, 1,000 kilogrammes in the second and 1,500 kilogrammes last year.

Even that amount was not enough.

“Our production has not been able to keep pace with demand,” said Chinimaya Gurung, chairperson of the cooperative. “Last year, we produced and sold 1,500 kilogrammes, but that was still far below what buyers were asking for.”

The cooperative’s storage facilities currently have no stock left. Every packet has been sold, while orders continue to come in from domestic and international markets.

For the women involved, the enterprise represents more than the commercialisation of a traditional food. It has given them a source of income and greater control over household finances.

“In the past, we depended on our husbands’ agricultural income to run our families and meet household expenses,” Gurung said. “Before we started producing and selling gundruk commercially, these women had no independent income. Having to depend on others for every expense was difficult.”

The idea of turning a food traditionally prepared for household consumption into a commercial product was initially unfamiliar to the women.

Some had worried about their families’ financial future and their children’s prospects, but they had little idea about what kind of enterprise they could establish in the village. They had the skills and access to mustard greens, but lacked business knowledge, capital and a clear plan.

The intervention of Green Foundation Nepal helped change that.

“We never believed that we could become successful entrepreneurs by selling gundruk,” said Pabitra Syangtan, a cooperative member. “Green Foundation Nepal helped us see the potential in a skill we already had.”

Hetauda Sub-Metropolitan City also provided support that helped the women turn the idea into a commercial operation, she said.

The women now manage a business built around a product that was once associated mainly with rural households and winter food shortages. Their work has also changed the economic role of women within the community.

Yet the cooperative faces a challenge that many small producers would welcome: demand is growing faster than its capacity to produce.

Increasing production will require more mustard greens, greater processing capacity and stronger distribution networks. For now, however, the women of Ghale Gaun are confronting the problem with a product that has been part of Nepali kitchens for generations.

What began as a method of preserving vegetables for the winter has become a means of earning income throughout the year. For the women of Ghale Gaun, gundruk is no longer simply a traditional food. It is their business.

The comprehensive training, initial grants and ongoing business support provided by Hetauda Sub-Metropolitan City changed how the women of Ghale Gaun viewed their own economic prospects. With new skills and confidence, they formally registered the Kanchanjunga Agriculture Cooperative Micro-Entrepreneur Industry, creating the institutional foundation for their business.

The women leased 15 katthas, about 0.5 hectares, of farmland at an annual rent of Rs1,500 per kattha and began growing mustard greens for gundruk production. But growing the crop proved easier than finding a market for the finished product.

“In our first year, the mustard harvest was very good, but we could not find a market,” said cooperative chair Gurung. “We did not have the required certification from the Department of Food Technology and Quality Control, so we could not sell our gundruk through supermarkets.”

Hundreds of thousands of rupees worth of gundruk accumulated in the cooperative’s storehouses, leaving the women worried that their investment could be lost.

The situation changed after Hetauda Sub-Metropolitan City helped the cooperative navigate the certification process. Once the women obtained the required government approval, demand rose sharply.

“Consumer trust increased as soon as we received the certification,” Gurung said. “The gundruk we had stored sold quickly. Traders and wholesalers started contacting us directly and orders began coming in.”

The women’s biggest concern has since changed from finding buyers to producing enough to meet demand.

The cooperative, which began with 11 women, now has 26 members. It currently cultivates mustard greens on 30 katthas of land and plans to expand to 50 katthas. The group hopes to create direct employment for more than 50 local women. Twenty women are currently employed by the enterprise.

The gundruk is sold in Makwanpur, Sindhuli, Bharatpur and Kathmandu. The cooperative has also received interest from Kathmandu-based exporters who plan to begin shipping the product to the United Kingdom next year, where it could find a market among Nepalis living abroad as well as consumers interested in traditional fermented foods.

As the business has expanded, the women have also found a way to reduce waste. Broken pieces and fine particles left over from gundruk production are processed into achar, a traditional Nepali pickle, with technical assistance from another non-governmental organisation.

The cooperative produced around 300 kilogrammes of the pickle this year, selling it for Rs1,000 per kilogramme and generating about Rs300,000 in revenue from the product. Its organic gundruk sells for Rs800 per kilogramme.

The women see growing demand for organic and chemical-free food as another opportunity. Their product also benefits from the nutritional value associated with fermented leafy greens.

Dr Hari Bahadur Khadka of Hetauda Hospital said gundruk contains dietary fibre, iron and calcium and can support digestion and gut health.

The cooperative’s success, however, has been measured in more than sales and production figures.

Women who once had little independent income now earn from an enterprise they collectively own and manage. Their greater financial independence has also increased their participation in household and community decisions.

“The commercial production of gundruk has changed not only the identity of our village but also the confidence and independence of our women,” said Lalit Ghalan, chief of the District Coordination Committee in Makwanpur and a resident of the ward.

Ghalan said the cooperative’s success shows how much can change when rural women get the support and opportunity to turn their skills into a business.

The cooperative began with a relatively modest investment: about Rs100,000 from Hetauda Sub-Metropolitan City and Rs80,000 contributed by its members. Three years later, a product once prepared mainly for household consumption has become a growing rural enterprise with ambitions beyond Nepal.

For the women of Ghale Gaun, the transformation is as much about control over their economic lives as it is about gundruk. A traditional food once made to help families survive the winter has become a means of creating jobs, building confidence and opening a path to markets far beyond their village.

articles.title: Hormuz Strait to remain shut until US meets interim deal conditions, Iran says
articles.summary:
The Strait of Hormuz will remain shut until the US meets the conditions ​of an interim deal signed with Iran in June, the top ‌Iranian negotiator Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said in comments published by state media on Tuesday.

These conditions include ​the US lifting its blockade of Iranian ports, lifting ​oil sanctions, releasing Tehran’s frozen assets, and ending threats and military operations on all fronts, Qalibaf told parliament.

The ​memorandum of understanding, clinched on June 17, quickly ​unravelled over a dispute about control of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which a fifth ​of global oil and liquefied natural gas ​flowed before the war.

US President Donald Trump said the ‌deal was “over” on July 7 and a week later Iran’s foreign ministry declared it “suspended”.

Under the MoU, Iran and the US had committed to ​negotiating a final ​deal — covering broader issues such as the fate of Iran’s nuclear programme — in ​a maximum of 60 days, extendable ​by mutual consent.

A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Monday that Iran would now shift to a “fully offensive” posture ⁠due ​to the stalled diplomatic ​efforts to secure a permanent end to the conflict.

articles.title: Four students swept away by flooded stream in Makawanpur
articles.summary:
Four students were swept away by the Basudev stream in Hetauda-19 of Makawanpur district on Tuesday while returning home from school, residents said.

The students were studying at Nirmal Secondary School in Hetauda-19 and were all below Grade 5, according to residents.

One of the students has been found dead, while search and rescue teams and residents are continuing to search for the other three.

articles.title: Mental wellbeing: When a parent goes abroad for work, children can feel a loss that has no end
articles.summary:
When a parent migrates for work, they leave behind fragments of their presence, which, for a child, are never quite enough to make up a whole person.

As parents’ migration for work becomes more normalised in Nepali society, we might be underestimating its psychological cost, a complex understanding of presence and absence in the children’s minds.

Through FaceTime, voice memos, pictures, and videos, their parent’s embrace is known but never truly felt. As a result, they neither become fully connected nor entirely foreign, leading to a sense of ambiguity in their grief.

Sunika Joshi is a mental health professional specialising in trauma, neurodiversity, child and adolescent mental health, and suicide prevention. She is also the co-founder of Lighthouse Neural, a mental health organisation.

Here, she discusses the psychological impact of parental migration on children, how prolonged separation can shape attachment and relationships, and what families can do to protect children’s emotional well-being.

When one parent goes abroad for work, what happens inside a child’s mind in the first few months before the ‘new normal’ sets in?

The new normal depends on who is the caretaker, living arrangements, and sense of security/ safety where they live. Usually, children gradually adapt to new family dynamics.

Initially, children may experience grief-like responses such as sadness, confusion, anger, and somatic complaints like headaches, stomach pain, and sleep issues.

Younger children may show stress in the form of bedwetting, anger issues, and crying over minor issues that are not related to the absence. Adolescents may experience increased worry due to uncertainty, loneliness, and fear.

It can be termed as ambiguous loss, which is a profound sense of loss and sadness that is not death-related; the parent is physically absent but psychologically or emotionally present in some way.

But at the same time, adolescents can also feel a sense of pride if they see it as a sacrifice for the family’s financial security and remain hopeful that their lives will improve—economically and socially.

If the child is young, has the family member explained what migration is and how the living arrangement will change? Is anyone helping the child to make sense of the change? Does the child have access to communicate with the parent who migrated? Questions, as such, matter equally.

There could be many underlying vulnerabilities. If the child has the right support, they can feel hopeful about the future, but if the child is exposed to uncertainty due to debt or illegal ways to go abroad, the risk of being cheated and the family being stressed, the child can also sense the stress and show emotional and behavioral symptoms.

How does prolonged physical absence affect a child’s attachment style? Are these kids more anxious, more avoidant, or does it vary?

What happens during the absence of the parent determines the attachment style. They can be anxious and avoidant. Prolonged separation can increase the risk of both.

Anxious attachment means becoming hypervigilant, fearing abandonment, and worrying about parents’ return, safety, and relationship. Experience emotional vulnerability and loneliness. This attachment happens when caregivers are unable to consistently meet or respond to the young child’s emotional and physical needs. Later in life, they might struggle with anxiety in relationships, making them ‘clingy’ or jealous.

Avoidant attachment means to learn to suppress and avoid emotional conversations, spending time with family, or communicating their issues. Children may become self-reliant and push people away; don’t actively seek out their caregiver for comfort or emotional support. It results when a young child loses a sense of security in their environment. It can lead to suspicion, hostility, and lack of commitment in later relationships.

But these depend on the child’s temperament, the consistency of the substitute caregiver and how communication with the absent parent is handled.

But when caregiving is inconsistent, children are likely to show anxiety, depressive symptoms, and challenges in forming an emotional bond with friends and family.

Can a strong emotional bond survive almost entirely through video calls and voice notes? What gets lost that even daily calls can't replace?

No, physical presence is different than talking on a call. You see the nuances. It is like reading a summary of the book without reading the entire book.

Video calls and voice notes help maintain a sense of connection and can reduce separation anxiety compared to no contact, but cannot fully replace physical presence, especially for younger children.

The child is deprived of physical affection, which is crucial for co-regulation, feeling safe and secure, and forming an attachment to the parent. The child and parent also miss out on the minor, firsthand details of daily routines and what each other's days look like.

Non-verbal communication is largely missing, creating a gap in understanding underlying emotions and in developing attachment through non-verbal cues. And if certain things are not communicated through words or messages, they will be missed.

In the Nepali context, emotional bonds are formed by providing material support in the form of favourite food and gifts. Families do not communicate through words and talk about emotions. In Nepal, fathers, in particular, do not share vulnerability or emotions.

So, this can create a huge gap in building a strong emotional bond as a family. Families would only know about each other through events shared across the device. What gets lost is the bond, trust, and reliability you create through physical presence, making memories by being in the same space and engaging in activities like cooking and celebrating festivals together. Also, passing down the culture, values, knowledge, and the roots of the family/ethnicity/indigeneity.

Is there any age range where a parent’s absence particularly leaves lasting damage?

Yes, in young age and in adolescence.

Younger children, when they have not made sense of the separation and do not understand the change, can show withdrawal and aggression. Early childhood is the time when they learn and understand attachment, love, care, affection, and emotion regulation from their parents, and disruptions in this process can have emotional consequences. Adolescents also face an increasing risk of confusion, loneliness, worry, and uncertainty.

As humans, we are all resilient and can adjust to change, but how a child makes sense of a parent's absence largely depends on the caretaker and guardian, as well as the family's response, the community the child lives in, and the environment.

The connection with the parent can become superficial and may lead to issues with socio-emotional adjustment. A sense of security and trust can also change as the child grows. Psychological well-being declines if more socio-economic challenges arise after migration.

What’s one piece of practical advice you’d give the parent staying behind to protect a child’s emotional development?

Choose a safe and secure place to live and a caregiver. Assess the risk of abuse, assault, discrimination, and neglect from the people around.

Do not pressure the child to take responsibility for the missing parent.

Make sure they understand why the parent migrated; do not expose them to the news of death, accidents, injury, parent separation.

Create space for the child to express their feelings, be vulnerable and if they are showing emotional distress, understand that it can be a reaction to worry and distress.

Do not shut the children and ask them to understand everything.

Help the child to foster a bond with the migrant parent- help them maintain a healthy relationship and communicate.

Avoid putting the child in the middle of adult conflicts about money or return plans.

Seek help from schools, communicate about the change in a child's life.

How does a child’s sense of self develop when one parent exists through a device or a photo rather than a physical presence?

A risk of getting detached from their culture and community surrounds them.

If they are living with relatives, they do not feel a sense of belonging to a family or community. The child will also find it difficult to navigate their emotions toward the parents; they may appreciate the sacrifice and see them as a hero or savior, or they may see them as not being part of the family's struggles and challenges in person.

There might be too much pressure on them to study well, to live with whatever is provided, and not ask for more.

Children also feel pressure to appreciate and repay the sacrifices their parents have made for their future by being overly pressured to excel academically, be smart, and be very ambitious.

This might not provide the child with an area to explore their authentic self, experiment with hobbies and strengths, and make room for any mistake or failure. So living in constant fear and worry and living up to the family’s expectations.

A sense of safety can be hampered.

If the children are taking the role of caretaker and replacing the parent who migrated, girls tend to start taking care of siblings, cooking and cleaning- all household chores. Sons might feel the responsibility for the family’s safety and security. There may be a mutual understanding of sharing struggles and burdens.

Is there a psychological difference between a parent who is dead, divorced, or absent due to migration?

Yes, migration is a different kind of grief. It is an ambiguous loss. The parent is alive and connected through video calls or messages but not present physically. It comes with uncertainty about when they will return, whether they are ever coming back, and also fear of separation from parents, breaking the family apart, and the uncertainty can prolong distress.

Children can also live in emotional conflict- they can feel guilty for being angry at the parent who sacrificed for the family and confused about what to feel.

Death is an irreversible loss and also a socially recognised loss followed by rituals according to the religion they follow. Grieving is mostly getting to terms with the fact that it is permanent and making sense of the loss- physically and emotionally.

Divorce is often breaking off the family dynamics; even if parents are present physically, it also comes with arrangements of who the child lives with and coming to terms with living separately, but both parents are alive.

Do these children struggle more with trust and intimacy later in life, in friendships or romantic relationships?

Trust and intimacy in later life—yes, it can create difficulty in forming strong relationships, trust and feeling secure.

Lower emotional closeness and less contact with parents and family. Causes difficulty trusting others and forming intimate relationships in adulthood. It can also show up in the form of fear of abandonment, getting into unhealthy relationships, and risk of addiction, and not understanding how relationships should be.

Either giving too much or giving too little. Can get into abusive relationships and not be able to recognise it or get out of it. Not understanding the emotional needs of a partner, as well as feeling like not being understood.

articles.title: Exhibit review: When an oral story becomes a painting
articles.summary:
Artist Bivas Rai’s solo exhibition ‘Myth & Memory’ will open at Siddhartha Art Gallery, Baber Mahal Revisited, on August 28.

Presented by the Australian Himalayan Foundation (AHF) and Siddhartha Art Gallery, the exhibition brings together paintings that explore Kirati Rai culture through Sakela, a communal dance and festival celebrated to honour nature and ancestors.

Rai, recipient of the 2025 AHF Himalayan Art Award, grew up in an extended Rai family surrounded by stories. As a child, however, he says he rarely had the patience to listen to them. Years later, his relationship with those stories has changed.

“Indigenous history is primarily passed down in the form of stories from one generation to the next,” says Rai. His growing curiosity about the stories he once avoided led him to spend the past year observing, listening to, and archiving accounts shared by elders in his family.

Rather than trying to establish a single authoritative version, ‘Myth & Memory’ works within this shifting nature of folklore.

Sakela provides the visual language for the series. Its silli, or dance movements, often imitate elements of nature, including animals and flowers. While Sakela sets the visual tone, Rai says the exhibition is rooted in sisterhood and matriarchy.

Every painting in the series features one of his sisters. Rai connects the women he grew up with to the Kirati myth of Tayama and Khiyama, the primordial sisters, allowing familial memory and inherited mythology to occupy the same space.

“My world has been shaped entirely by the strength and presence of my mother, her sisters, and my own sisters,” says Rai.

Through ‘Myth & Memory’, these recollections are carried from oral storytelling into painting, preserving them while acknowledging that memory itself continues to shift each time a story is retold.

The exhibition will be inaugurated by Australian Ambassador to Nepal Simon Ernst, AHF Chair Garry Weare, and AHF Himalayan Art Award founder Margie Thomas.

Myth & Memory

When: August 28 to September 20Where: Siddhartha Art Gallery, Baber Mahal Revisited, KathmanduOpening: August 28, 5:30 pm

articles.title: Sikkim chief minister unveils ticket, T-shirt for Nepathya concert
articles.summary:
Nepal’s folk-rock band Nepathya’s upcoming concert in Sikkim has received official backing from the state government, with Chief Minister Prem Singh Tamang –Golay, unveiling the event’s ticket and specially designed T-shirt.

Tamang launched the two items during a ceremony in Gangtok on Saturday marking India’s 80th Republic Day. Nepathya had earlier announced that it would perform at Paljor Stadium in the Sikkim capital on October 31.

The concert will be the band’s fourth performance in Sikkim and its biggest there to date, according to the organisers. Nepathya’s first concert in the state was held indoors after the band’s return to the music scene. Its subsequent outdoor performances took place in Pakyong, on the grounds opposite St Xavier’s School, and Rabangla, on the shore of Cho Jo Lake.

Organised by Positive Vibes Entertainment Network, the Gangtok concert aims to promote Sikkim’s music and culture, encourage young people’s creativity and showcase the state’s natural beauty, the organisers said.

Tenzing Dorje, coordinator of the organising team, thanked Tamang for publicly supporting the event.

“We are eagerly looking forward to welcoming Nepathya, one of Nepal’s leading musical groups, to Sikkim,” Dorje said.

Nepathya lead singer Amrit Gurung said the band had consistently received a warm reception in Sikkim and Darjeeling, where several generations have grown up listening to its songs on local radio stations.

“We have been receiving encouraging news about the concert for quite some time, which has further boosted our enthusiasm,” Gurung said.

Nepathya will also perform in Itahari on November 4 and is preparing for a concert in Kirtipur. The band is scheduled to tour South Korea this year and is planning performances in several Nepali cities and abroad towards the end of the year.

Gurung will be joined in Gangtok by Dhruv Lama on drums, Subin Shakya on bass guitar, Niraj Gurung on guitar, Shanti Rayamajhi on madal and Dineshraj Regmi on keyboards.

Tickets for the Gangtok concert can be purchased online through Nepathya’s official website.

articles.title: Budget-friendly places for Nepali students in Hamilton
articles.summary:
Hillcrest functions as the primary campus neighbourhood for Hamilton, operating essentially as the city's main student hub. Rather than a quiet suburban zone, Hillcrest is highly energetic and packed with student flats, local takeaways, and young people walking to lectures. The neighbourhood is completely dominated by university culture, making it the central gathering point for the local international student community.

People can save time and money because they can walk to classes and the university library within minutes, completely eliminating daily bus or parking costs.

Housing demand is incredibly high at the start of semesters, meaning competition for good rooms is fierce, and properties can suffer from student-related noise.

Silverdale serves as a peaceful alternative to the busier streets of Hamilton. It functions as a relaxed retreat where students can study quietly but still reach campus in under five minutes.

Rents are reasonable, and the neighbourhood offers a much calmer, quieter environment that is perfect for focused study.

The area lacks its own major nightlife or dining scene, so people will have to travel to neighbouring suburbs for entertainment or grocery shopping.

Nawton is a well-established residential suburb located on the western side of Hamilton, far from the main university campus. It serves as an excellent hideaway for budget-conscious students who want to escape the university bubble completely.

Weekly rental prices here are among the lowest in the entire city, letting you get a much larger room or property for a lower price.

The commute to the university is long and requires catching a bus through the city centre.

Dinsdale sits elevated on the western hills of Hamilton, acting as a highly independent and fully self-contained suburban community. Rather than just a collection of houses, it features its own comprehensive shopping centres, supermarkets, and medical clinics that cater to all daily needs.

Access to the local amenities means people can buy cheap groceries and essentials right on their doorstep.

Distance from the eastern campus means people are completely dependent on public transport schedules or owning a car to get to their classes.

Hamilton East

Hamilton East is one of the city’s oldest and most character-filled suburbs, blending a trendy heritage vibe with student living. It serves as a creative bridge perfectly positioned right between the university campus and the central business district.

It offers the lifestyle balance in Hamilton, giving students immediate access to food, local employment opportunities, and vibrant weekend river walks.

The charming, older character homes can be poorly insulated, making them quite cold and expensive to heat during the damp winter months.

Based on conversations with local Nepali students in Hamilton.

articles.title: Two Nepalis killed on Romanian railway track
articles.summary:
Two Nepalis were killed after being hit by a train in Romania’s eastern city of Bacău early Sunday morning. Their identities have not yet been disclosed.

According to a statement from the Bacău Inspectorate for Emergency Situations (ISU), the two were struck by a train at around 3:21 am while walking along the railway line near Chimiei Street.

Emergency responders, including ambulances, rescue teams and medical personnel, reached the site shortly after receiving information about the incident. They found both individuals dead upon arrival, the ISU said.

Romanian police and railway authorities have launched an investigation into the accident.

“An investigation is underway to establish how they ended up on the railway line and the circumstances that led to the accident,” the ISU said in its statement.

articles.title: Australia tightens student visa rules, rejects 64 percent of Nepali applications
articles.summary:
Australia has rejected around 64 percent of offshore student visa applications from Nepal, marking the highest rejection rate recorded for Nepali applicants, according to official data.

The surge in visa refusals comes after the Australian government tightened its screening process for international students amid concerns over migration levels, housing pressures and the integrity of the education system.

Australia categorises countries under an “Evidence Level” risk framework to determine the level of scrutiny applied during visa processing. Education sector insiders say Nepal was recently moved to “Level 3”, the highest-risk category, from “Level 2” following a government review conducted several months ago.

The impact has been most severe in the vocational education and training (VET) sector, which traditionally attracts students seeking shorter and more affordable courses. Nearly 90 percent of Nepali applications for VET courses have been rejected, with only 56 of 549 applicants receiving visas, according to recent statistics.

Around 60,000 Nepali students are currently enrolled in Australian institutions. Of them, about 56,000 are existing students, while roughly 4,000 are new arrivals.

Data from Australia’s Department of Home Affairs shows a sharp decline in new student arrivals from Nepal. Between January and May this year, only 2,700 of 7,500 offshore applicants from Nepal were granted visas. During the same period last year, 7,167 of 8,028 applicants received approvals.

The uncertainty surrounding visa approvals, combined with rising application costs, has discouraged many prospective students. Applicants currently have to pay an application fee of A$2,500 (approximately Rs260,000), which is non-refundable even if the visa is rejected.

Sanjeev Pandey, a Sydney-based lawyer, said Australia had welcomed a large number of international students after the Covid-19 pandemic, but authorities later became concerned about patterns of students changing courses and extending their stay without completing their original programmes.

“The government may have also tightened student visa rules to address growing employment and housing pressures,” Pandey said.

The stricter visa regime has raised concerns among education consultancies and smaller institutions that rely heavily on international enrolments.

Khagendra Satyal, international business development manager at Central Australian College, said the decline in student arrivals had significantly affected the sector.

“Visas are now granted only after assessing what positive contributions an international student can make to Australia in the long run,” Satyal said. “Students applying from Nepal need to understand this shift.”

The immigration crackdown also comes amid growing political pressure in Australia over migration. Analysts say the rise of politicians with hardline positions on immigration, including Pauline Hanson, has contributed to a broader political push for tighter controls.
